Build Snippetbox: a web app for pasting and sharing snippets of text. Chapter one sets the destination and the toolchain; chapter two builds the whole foundations of the app — modules, routing, headers, query strings, project structure, templates and static files. Let’s Go: Learn to build professional web applications with Go Alex Edwards · 2nd edition · version 2.20.0, last updated 2023-02-17 · 426 pages. Chapter one is the on-ramp: what we’re building, what you need installed, and how to read the code samples.

The chapter

“In this book we’ll be building a web application called Snippetbox.”

Snippetbox lets people paste and share snippets of text — a bit like Pastebin or GitHub’s Gists. By the end of the book it looks like the screenshot below: a “Create a New Snippet” page with a title field, a content box, a Delete in choice of one year / one week / one day, and a green Publish snippet button.

The application starts off super simple, with just one web page. Then with each chapter it’s built up step-by-step until a user can save and view snippets through the app. That journey covers how to structure a project, routing requests, working with a database, processing forms and displaying dynamic data safely.

Later in the book user accounts are added, and the application is restricted so that only registered users can create snippets — which brings in configuring a HTTPS server, session management, user authentication and middleware.

Figure 1.1 — the finished app

Why show the end first? Everything in chapters 2–15 is a step towards this one form. Keeping the screenshot in mind makes the incremental refactors — a handler, then a servemux, then templates, then a database — feel like progress rather than churn.

Prerequisites — background knowledge

The book is designed for people who are new to Go, but it’s more enjoyable if you have a general understanding of Go’s syntax first. If you find yourself struggling with the syntax, The Little Go Book by Karl Seguin is a fantastic tutorial, and for something more interactive the Tour of Go is the recommendation.

You’re also expected to have a (very) basic understanding of HTML/CSS and SQL, and some familiarity with using a terminal. If you’ve built a web application in any other language before — Ruby, Python, PHP or C# — the book is a good fit.

  • Go syntax basics
  • Basic HTML & CSS
  • Basic SQL
  • Comfortable in a terminal

Helpful links from the chapter: The Little Go Book · A Tour of Go

Prerequisites — Go 1.20

The book is correct for the latest major release of Go (version 1.20), and that’s the version to install if you want to code along. If Go is already installed, check it from the terminal with go version:

Prerequisites — other software

A few other bits of software should be available if you want to follow along fully:

  1. curl — for working with HTTP requests and responses from your terminal. On macOS and Linux it’s usually pre-installed or in your software repositories; otherwise download the latest version.
  2. A web browser with good developer tools — the book uses Firefox, but Chromium, Chrome or Microsoft Edge work just as well.
  3. Your favourite text editor — the chapter ends there, mid-sentence, because any editor will do.

How to read the book

Chapter one also sets the conventions used throughout — worth knowing before you copy a single line.

Code blocks have a silver background; long blocks may replace irrelevant parts with an ellipsis. Most blocks carry a title bar naming the file you’re working on:

File: hello.gogo
package main

... // Indicates that some existing code has been omitted.

func sayHello() {
    fmt.Println("Hello world!")
}

Terminal instructions have a black background and start with a dollar sign. They work on any Unix-based system, macOS and Linux alike; sample output appears in silver beneath the command:

Terminalshell
$ echo "Hello world!"
Hello world!

On Windows, substitute the DOS equivalent or use the normal Windows GUI. Some chapters finish with an additional information section that isn’t needed for the build but is still important — very new Gophers can skip those and circle back later.

Hint from the book: if you’re following along with the application build, use the HTML version of the book rather than the PDF or EPUB. It works in all browsers, and the formatting of code blocks is retained if you want to copy-and-paste code directly.

Chapter 2 — Foundations

“Alright, let’s get started!”

Chapter 2 builds the entire skeleton of Snippetbox in nine sections. By the end of page 61 the application has a project layout that scales, a servemux with three routes, method-restricted handlers with custom headers, validated query strings, an inherited HTML template set, a static file server and a working understanding of the http.Handler interface.

It opens by listing exactly that:

  • Set up a project directory following Go conventions
  • Start a web server and listen for requests
  • Route requests by path
  • Send different responses, headers and status codes
  • Fetch and validate untrusted query-string input
  • Structure the project sensibly
  • Render HTML with template inheritance
  • Serve static files

2.1 · Project setup and creating a module

Everything lives in a snippetbox directory in $HOME/code. The next decision is the module path — a canonical, globally unique identifier for the project. The convention is to base it on a URL you own; the book uses snippetbox.alexedwards.net.

Terminalshell
$ mkdir -p $HOME/code/snippetbox
$ cd $HOME/code/snippetbox
$ go mod init snippetbox.alexedwards.net
go: creating new go.mod: module snippetbox.alexedwards.net
File: go.modgo.mod
module snippetbox.alexedwards.net

go 1.20

Modules make third-party dependencies manageable, help avoid supply-chain attacks and give reproducible builds. To prove the toolchain works, the book adds the traditional first program and runs it with go run ., which compiles to a binary in /tmp and executes it in one step. (go run ., go run main.go and go run snippetbox.alexedwards.net are all equivalent here.)

File: main.gogo
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Hello world!")
}

Additional information. If your project can be downloaded by other people, the module path should equal the URL it is downloaded from — a package hosted at https://github.com/foo/bar gets the module path github.com/foo/bar.

2.2 · Web application basics

Three components make a web application: a handler (think: controller — runs logic and writes headers and a body), a router (Go calls it a servemux; it maps URL patterns to handlers) and a web server. In Go the server is part of your program — no Nginx or Apache required.

File: main.gogo
package main

import (
    "log"
    "net/http"
)

// Define a home handler function which writes a byte slice containing
// "Hello from Snippetbox" as the response body.
func home(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.Write([]byte("Hello from Snippetbox"))
}

func main() {
    // Use the http.NewServeMux() function to initialize a new servemux, then
    // register the home function as the handler for the "/" URL pattern.
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("/", home)

    // Use the http.ListenAndServe() function to start a new web server. We pass in
    // two parameters: the TCP network address to listen on (in this case ":4000")
    // and the servemux we just created. If http.ListenAndServe() returns an error
    // we use the log.Fatal() function to log the error message and exit. Note
    // that any error returned by http.ListenAndServe() is always non-nil.
    log.Print("Starting server on :4000")
    err := http.ListenAndServe(":4000", mux)
    log.Fatal(err)
}

Important. Go’s servemux treats the pattern "/" as a catch-all, so /foo returns the same page. Stop the server with Ctrl+c. The address format for http.ListenAndServe() is "host:port"; omitting the host listens on every interface.

2.3 · Routing requests

One route is not much of an app, so two more are registered — the table the book has just introduced:

URL patternHandlerAction
/homeDisplay the home page
/snippet/viewsnippetViewDisplay a specific snippet
/snippet/createsnippetCreateCreate a new snippet
File: main.gogo
// Add a snippetView handler function.
func snippetView(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.Write([]byte("Display a specific snippet..."))
}

// Add a snippetCreate handler function.
func snippetCreate(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.Write([]byte("Create a new snippet..."))
}

func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("/", home)
    mux.HandleFunc("/snippet/view", snippetView)
    mux.HandleFunc("/snippet/create", snippetCreate)

    log.Print("Starting server on :4000")
    err := http.ListenAndServe(":4000", mux)
    log.Fatal(err)
}

Fixed paths vs. subtree paths

Patterns without a trailing slash are fixed paths — matched only on an exact URL match. Patterns with a trailing slash are subtree paths — matched when the start of the URL matches, as if a wildcard sat at the end ("/**", "/static/**"). That is precisely why "/" behaves as a catch-all: it means “one slash, then anything or nothing”.

Go won’t let you change that behaviour, so the fix lives in the handler: check r.URL.Path and return http.NotFound() before writing anything.

File: main.gogo
func home(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    // Check if the current request URL path exactly matches "/". If it doesn't, use
    // the http.NotFound() function to send a 404 response to the client.
    // Importantly, we then return from the handler. If we don't return the handler
    // would keep executing and also write the "Hello from SnippetBox" message.
    if r.URL.Path != "/" {
        http.NotFound(w, r)
        return
    }
    w.Write([]byte("Hello from Snippetbox"))
}

The DefaultServeMux

http.HandleFunc() registers routes without an explicit servemux, using a package-level global:

From the Go sourcego
var DefaultServeMux = NewServeMux()

The book advises against it for production: because it is global, any imported third-party package can register a route on it — and a compromised dependency could expose a malicious handler. Use a locally scoped servemux.

Additional information. Longer patterns always win, so registration order is irrelevant. Paths are sanitised (/foo/bar/..//baz → 301 to /foo/baz). A request for a registered subtree path without its trailing slash gets a 301 with the slash added. Patterns may include host names ("foo.example.org/"), which are checked before non-host patterns. And the servemux is deliberately lightweight: no method-based routing, no variables in URLs, no regexp — third-party routers cover those.

2.4 · Customizing HTTP headers

/snippet/create becomes a POST-only route. Later it will write to a database — a non-idempotent action — so HTTP good practice says restrict it now.

MethodPatternHandlerAction
ANY/homeDisplay the home page
ANY/snippet/viewsnippetViewDisplay a specific snippet
POST/snippet/createsnippetCreateCreate a new snippet

The first version sends the status code explicitly. Two nuances matter: w.WriteHeader() can only be called once, and if you don’t call it at all the first w.Write() sends 200 OK automatically — so a non-200 status must be written before any body.

File: main.go — first attemptgo
func snippetCreate(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != "POST" {
        w.WriteHeader(405)
        w.Write([]byte("Method Not Allowed"))
        return
    }
    w.Write([]byte("Create a new snippet..."))
}
Terminal — before and aftershell
$ curl -i -X POST http://localhost:4000/snippet/create
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Sat, 29 Jan 2022 10:27:14 GMT
Content-Length: 23
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

Create a new snippet...

$ curl -i -X PUT http://localhost:4000/snippet/create
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Date: Sat, 29 Jan 2022 10:27:55 GMT
Content-Length: 18
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

Method Not Allowed

Then the Allow header is added — a hint to clients about which methods the URL supports — followed by the http.Error() shortcut, which sets the status and body for us, and finally the net/http constants, which remove the typos waiting inside "POST" and 405. That last version is the finished handler:

File: main.go — final versiongo
func snippetCreate(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
        w.Header().Set("Allow", http.MethodPost)
        http.Error(w, "Method Not Allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
        return
    }
    w.Write([]byte("Create a new snippet..."))
}
Terminal — with the Allow headershell
$ curl -i -X PUT http://localhost:4000/snippet/create
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Allow: POST
Date: Sat, 29 Jan 2022 10:29:12 GMT
Content-Length: 18
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8

Method Not Allowed

Important. Changing the header map after WriteHeader() or Write() has no effect — all headers must be set first.

Header mechanics from the additional information. Go sets Date, Content-Length and Content-Type itself; the content type comes from http.DetectContentType(), which cannot tell JSON from plain text, so JSON needs an explicit w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json"). The map supports Set/Add/Del/Get/Values; names are canonicalised (case-insensitive) unless you write to the underlying map[string][]string directly — which is also the only way to suppress a system header, by setting it to nil.

Header map operationsgo
// Set a new cache-control header. If an existing "Cache-Control" header exists
// it will be overwritten.
w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=31536000")

// In contrast, the Add() method appends a new "Cache-Control" header and can
// be called multiple times.
w.Header().Add("Cache-Control", "public")
w.Header().Add("Cache-Control", "max-age=31536000")

// Delete all values for the "Cache-Control" header.
w.Header().Del("Cache-Control")

// Retrieve the first value for the "Cache-Control" header.
w.Header().Get("Cache-Control")

// Retrieve a slice of all values for the "Cache-Control" header.
w.Header().Values("Cache-Control")

// Suppress a system-generated header.
w.Header()["Date"] = nil

2.5 · URL query strings

snippetView learns to accept ?id=1. The value is untrusted user input, so it is converted with strconv.Atoi() and validated to be a positive integer; anything else gets a 404.

File: main.gogo
import (
    "fmt" // New import
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "strconv" // New import
)

func snippetView(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    // Extract the value of the id parameter from the query string and try to
    // convert it to an integer using the strconv.Atoi() function. If it can't
    // be converted to an integer, or the value is less than 1, we return a 404 page
    // not found response.
    id, err := strconv.Atoi(r.URL.Query().Get("id"))
    if err != nil || id < 1 {
        http.NotFound(w, r)
        return
    }

    // Use the fmt.Fprintf() function to interpolate the id value with our response
    // and write it to the http.ResponseWriter.
    fmt.Fprintf(w, "Display a specific snippet with ID %d...", id)
}

Why fmt.Fprintf(w, …) compiles. It wants an io.Writer…

io.Writergo
func Fprintf(w io.Writer, format string, a ...any) (n int, err error)

…yet an http.ResponseWriter is accepted, because it satisfies the interface by having a Write() method. In practice: anywhere you see an io.Writer, you can pass the response writer, and whatever is written becomes the response body.

2.6 · Project structure and organization

There is no single correct layout for Go web apps. The advice: don’t over-complicate; add structure only when it is demonstrably needed. This project follows a widely used outline.

Terminalshell
$ cd $HOME/code/snippetbox
$ rm main.go
$ mkdir -p cmd/web internal ui/html ui/static
$ touch cmd/web/main.go
$ touch cmd/web/handlers.go

Two benefits: Go and non-Go assets are cleanly separated (the root stays free for UI files, makefiles and module definitions), and the layout scales — a future CLI would sit at cmd/cli and import everything under internal. Note that internal is special in Go: packages beneath it can only be imported by code inside the parent of internal — that is, only by this project.

File: cmd/web/handlers.gogo
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "strconv"
)

func home(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.URL.Path != "/" {
        http.NotFound(w, r)
        return
    }
    w.Write([]byte("Hello from Snippetbox"))
}

func snippetView(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    id, err := strconv.Atoi(r.URL.Query().Get("id"))
    if err != nil || id < 1 {
        http.NotFound(w, r)
        return
    }
    fmt.Fprintf(w, "Display a specific snippet with ID %d...", id)
}

func snippetCreate(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
        w.Header().Set("Allow", http.MethodPost)
        http.Error(w, "Method Not Allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
        return
    }
    w.Write([]byte("Create a new snippet..."))
}
Terminalshell
$ go run ./cmd/web
2022/01/29 12:02:26 Starting server on :4000

2.7 · HTML templating and inheritance

Time for a real home page. Over the next chapters it becomes the page sketched below; first comes a template at ui/html/pages/home.tmpl and a handler that parses and executes it with html/template — the package that parses and renders templates safely.

File: ui/html/pages/home.tmpl — first versionhtml
<!doctype html>
<html lang='en'>
    <head>
        <meta charset='utf-8'>
        <title>Home - Snippetbox</title>
    </head>
    <body>
        <header>
            <h1><a href='/'>Snippetbox</a></h1>
        </header>
        <main>
            <h2>Latest Snippets</h2>
            <p>There's nothing to see here yet!</p>
        </main>
        <footer>Powered by <a href='https://golang.org/'>Go</a></footer>
    </body>
</html>

Note. .tmpl means nothing to Go — it just makes template files recognisable. .html or .tmpl.html work too, the latter helping editors with syntax highlighting.

File: cmd/web/handlers.go — rendering itgo
func home(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.URL.Path != "/" {
        http.NotFound(w, r)
        return
    }

    // Use the template.ParseFiles() function to read the template file into a
    // template set. If there's an error, we log the detailed error message and use
    // the http.Error() function to send a generic 500 Internal Server Error
    // response to the user.
    ts, err := template.ParseFiles("./ui/html/pages/home.tmpl")
    if err != nil {
        log.Print(err.Error())
        http.Error(w, "Internal Server Error", 500)
        return
    }

    // We then use the Execute() method on the template set to write the
    // template content as the response body. The last parameter to Execute()
    // represents any dynamic data that we want to pass in, which for now we'll
    // leave as nil.
    err = ts.Execute(w, nil)
    if err != nil {
        log.Print(err.Error())
        http.Error(w, "Internal Server Error", 500)
    }
}

Template composition

Every page will share a header, nav and metadata, so that boilerplate moves into a base template with holes in it. {{define "base"}} defines a named template; {{template "title" .}} and {{template "main" .}} invoke other named templates (the dot is the data passed to them).

File: ui/html/base.tmplgo template
{{define "base"}}
<!doctype html>
<html lang='en'>
    <head>
        <meta charset='utf-8'>
        <title>{{template "title" .}} - Snippetbox</title>
    </head>
    <body>
        <header>
            <h1><a href='/'>Snippetbox</a></h1>
        </header>
        <main>
            {{template "main" .}}
        </main>
        <footer>Powered by <a href='https://golang.org/'>Go</a></footer>
    </body>
</html>
{{end}}
File: ui/html/pages/home.tmpl — defines the holesgo template
{{define "title"}}Home{{end}}

{{define "main"}}
    <h2>Latest Snippets</h2>
    <p>There's nothing to see here yet!</p>
{{end}}
File: cmd/web/handlers.go — parse both, execute "base"go
// Initialize a slice containing the paths to the two files. It's important
// to note that the file containing our base template must be the *first*
// file in the slice.
files := []string{
    "./ui/html/base.tmpl",
    "./ui/html/pages/home.tmpl",
}

ts, err := template.ParseFiles(files...)
if err != nil {
    log.Print(err.Error())
    http.Error(w, "Internal Server Error", 500)
    return
}

// Use the ExecuteTemplate() method to write the content of the "base"
// template as the response body.
err = ts.ExecuteTemplate(w, "base", nil)

The template set now holds three named templates — base, title and main — and ExecuteTemplate(w, "base", nil) renders the composition.

Embedding partials

Reusable fragments go in their own files. The navigation bar becomes ui/html/partials/nav.tmpl, invoked with {{template "nav" .}} from the base template and added to the files slice.

File: ui/html/partials/nav.tmplgo template
{{define "nav"}}
    <nav>
        <a href='/'>Home</a>
    </nav>
{{end}}

Additional information. {{block "name" .}}…{{end}} works like {{template}} but supplies default content when the invoked template is missing from the set — handy for optional sidebars. With nothing between block and end, the invoked template becomes entirely optional. Go’s embed package can also bake files into the binary instead of reading them from disk; the book returns to that later.

2.8 · Serving static files

CSS, images and a little JavaScript arrive in ui/static, then http.FileServer serves them. Because the file server strips the leading slash and looks up the remainder inside the given directory, the /static prefix must be removed first — http.StripPrefix() does exactly that.

Terminalshell
$ curl https://www.alexedwards.net/static/sb-v2.tar.gz | tar -xvz -C ./ui/static/
File: cmd/web/main.gogo
func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()

    // Create a file server which serves files out of the "./ui/static" directory.
    // Note that the path given to the http.Dir function is relative to the project
    // directory root.
    fileServer := http.FileServer(http.Dir("./ui/static/"))

    // Use the mux.Handle() function to register the file server as the handler for
    // all URL paths that start with "/static/". For matching paths, we strip the
    // "/static" prefix before the request reaches the file server.
    mux.Handle("/static/", http.StripPrefix("/static", fileServer))

    // Register the other application routes as normal.
    mux.HandleFunc("/", home)
    mux.HandleFunc("/snippet/view", snippetView)
    mux.HandleFunc("/snippet/create", snippetCreate)

    log.Print("Starting server on :4000")
    err := http.ListenAndServe(":4000", mux)
    log.Fatal(err)
}

Finally the base template links the stylesheet, the favicon, the Ubuntu Mono webfont and the JavaScript file — and the page comes alive:

File: ui/html/base.tmpl — head and body additionsgo template
<!-- Link to the CSS stylesheet and favicon -->
<link rel='stylesheet' href='/static/css/main.css'>
<link rel='shortcut icon' href='/static/img/favicon.ico' type='image/x-icon'>

<!-- Also link to some fonts hosted by Google -->
<link rel='stylesheet' href='https://fonts.googleapis.com/css?family=Ubuntu+Mono:400,700'>

...

<!-- And include the JavaScript file -->
<script src="/static/js/main.js" type="text/javascript"></script>

Additional information. The file server cleans every path with path.Clean() (blocking directory traversal), supports Range requests — curl -H "Range: bytes=100-199" returns 206 Partial Content — handles Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since with 304 Not Modified, and sets Content-Type from the extension via mime.TypeByExtension(). Frequently served files are usually read from the OS cache rather than disk. For one-off files use http.ServeFile() — but it does not sanitise paths, so clean untrusted input with filepath.Clean(). To disable directory listings, drop a blank index.html in each directory, or implement a custom http.FileSystem that returns os.ErrNotExist for directories.

2.9 · The http.Handler interface

Strictly, a handler is any object satisfying this interface:

net/httpgo
type Handler interface {
    ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, *Request)
}

So the minimum handler is any type with a ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) method — a struct, a string, anything:

A handler typego
type home struct{}

func (h *home) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.Write([]byte("This is my home page"))
}

mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.Handle("/", &home{})

Creating an object just to hang a method on is long-winded, which is why handlers are written as plain functions. Such a function is not itself a handler — the http.HandlerFunc() adapter adds the ServeHTTP() method for you:

Function → handlergo
mux.Handle("/", http.HandlerFunc(home))   // what HandleFunc() does for us
mux.HandleFunc("/", home)              // ...so we normally write this

Chaining handlers

http.ListenAndServe(addr string, handler Handler) wants a Handler — and a servemux qualifies, because it has a ServeHTTP() method too. The servemux is best understood as a special handler that passes the request to a second handler instead of answering itself. A Go web app is a chain of ServeHTTP() calls; middleware later in the book extends the chain.

Requests are handled concurrently. Every incoming request is served in its own goroutine. That is a large part of why Go servers are fast — and why shared state accessed from handlers needs protecting against race conditions.

Chapter 3 — Configuration and error handling

“Housekeeping”

Chapter 3 adds almost no functionality. Instead it reorganises the application so it can grow: configuration comes from flags, logging gets levels, dependencies are injected through an application struct, errors are centralised in helpers, and the routes move out of main(). It is the chapter that turns a working demo into something maintainable.

No figures in this chapter. Pages 62–85 are text and code only — the first chapter of the book without a single screenshot. Everything below is code the book prints, and each section links to the same behaviour running live in the demo.

3.1 · Managing configuration settings

main.go currently hard-codes two settings: the network address ":4000" and the static directory "./ui/static". That mixes configuration with code and makes it impossible to use different settings in development, testing and production. Go’s idiomatic fix is a command-line flag:

Terminalshell
$ go run ./cmd/web -addr=":80"
Defining the flaggo
addr := flag.String("addr", ":4000", "HTTP network address")

That line names the flag, sets its default and documents it. The value lands in addr at runtime — but only after flag.Parse() is called, and before the variable is used. The returned value is a pointer, hence the dereference when the address is used:

File: cmd/web/main.gogo
import (
    "flag" // New import
    "log"
    "net/http"
)

func main() {
    // Define a new command-line flag with the name 'addr', a default value of ":4000"
    // and some short help text explaining what the flag controls. The value of the
    // flag will be stored in the addr variable at runtime.
    addr := flag.String("addr", ":4000", "HTTP network address")

    // Importantly, we use the flag.Parse() function to parse the command-line flag.
    // This reads in the command-line flag value and assigns it to the addr
    // variable. You need to call this *before* you use the addr variable
    // otherwise it will always contain the default value of ":4000". If any errors are
    // encountered during parsing the application will be terminated.
    flag.Parse()

    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    fileServer := http.FileServer(http.Dir("./ui/static/"))
    mux.Handle("/static/", http.StripPrefix("/static", fileServer))

    mux.HandleFunc("/", home)
    mux.HandleFunc("/snippet/view", snippetView)
    mux.HandleFunc("/snippet/create", snippetCreate)

    // The value returned from the flag.String() function is a pointer to the flag
    // value, not the value itself. So we need to dereference the pointer (i.e.
    // prefix it with the * symbol) before using it. Note that we're using the
    // log.Printf() function to interpolate the address with the log message.
    log.Printf("Starting server on %s", *addr)
    err := http.ListenAndServe(*addr, mux)
    log.Fatal(err)
}

Three things worth knowing about flags: they are optional (omitting -addr falls back to ":4000"), they convert types automatically (flag.Int(), flag.Bool(), flag.Float64() fail fast on a bad value), and -help lists them all with the help text — free documentation:

Terminalshell
$ go run ./cmd/web -addr=":9999"
2022/01/29 15:50:20 Starting server on :9999

$ go run ./cmd/web -help
Usage of /tmp/go-build3672328037/b001/exe/web:
  -addr string
        HTTP network address (default ":4000")

Additional information. Environment variables look tempting, but os.Getenv() gives no default, no -help and always a string. The book’s compromise is to pass the environment variable as a flag: go run ./cmd/web -addr=$SNIPPETBOX_ADDR. Booleans accept a bare -flag (equal to -flag=true), and flag.StringVar() can parse directly into a field of a config struct. Ports 0–1023 need root, and give bind: permission denied.

Live: the demo server implements the same flag set. /config shows the values it actually parsed; node web/server.js -help prints the equivalent usage block.

3.2 · Leveled logging

So far logging uses the standard logger via log.Printf() and log.Fatal(), which stamps everything the same way and sends it all to stderr. The application has two kinds of message — informational and errors — and they deserve different treatment: INFO to stdout, ERROR to stderr with the calling file and line. Two custom loggers do it:

File: cmd/web/main.go — the two loggersgo
// Use log.New() to create a logger for writing information messages. This takes
// three parameters: the destination to write the logs to (os.Stdout), a string
// prefix for message (INFO followed by a tab), and flags to indicate what
// additional information to include (local date and time). Note that the flags
// are joined using the bitwise OR operator |.
infoLog := log.New(os.Stdout, "INFO\t", log.Ldate|log.Ltime)

// Create a logger for writing error messages in the same way, but use stderr as
// the destination and use the log.Lshortfile flag to include the relevant
// file name and line number.
errorLog := log.New(os.Stderr, "ERROR\t", log.Ldate|log.Ltime|log.Lshortfile)

infoLog.Printf("Starting server on %s", *addr)
err := http.ListenAndServe(*addr, mux)
errorLog.Fatal(err)

Running a second copy of the server produces the two prefixes side by side, and note the main.go:37 on the error line:

Terminal — the address is already in useshell
$ go run ./cmd/web
INFO    2022/01/29 16:00:50 Starting server on :4000
ERROR   2022/01/29 16:00:50 main.go:37: listen tcp :4000: bind: address already in use
exit status 1

Because the loggers write to the standard streams, logging stays decoupled from the application: the execution environment decides where the output ends up, simply by redirecting it.

Terminal — redirecting the streamsshell
$ go run ./cmd/web >>/tmp/info.log 2>>/tmp/error.log

One loose end: Go’s HTTP server logs its own problems with the standard logger. Wrapping the server in an http.Server struct lets it share errorLog:

File: cmd/web/main.go — replacing ListenAndServe()go
// Initialize a new http.Server struct. We set the Addr and Handler fields so
// that the server uses the same network address and routes as before, and set
// the ErrorLog field so that the server now uses the custom errorLog logger in
// the event of any problems.
srv := &http.Server{
    Addr:     *addr,
    ErrorLog: errorLog,
    Handler:  mux,
}

infoLog.Printf("Starting server on %s", *addr)
err := srv.ListenAndServe()
errorLog.Fatal(err)

Additional information. Avoid Panic() and Fatal() outside main() — return errors instead. Loggers from log.New() are concurrency-safe, so one logger can be shared across goroutines and handlers; if several loggers share a destination, that Write() must be safe too. log.Llongfile gives the full path and log.LUTC forces UTC timestamps.

Live: /logs streams this server’s real stdout/stderr output — INFO lines without a file reference, ERROR lines with one, exactly like the book.

3.3 · Dependency injection

The home handler still calls log.Print(), i.e. the standard logger, instead of the new errorLog. How does a handler in handlers.go reach a value created in main()? The same question applies to every future dependency: a database pool, a template cache, a session manager.

Globals are the simplest answer and the wrong one — they are implicit, error-prone and hard to test. Instead, put the dependencies in a struct and make the handlers methods on it:

File: cmd/web/main.go — the application structgo
// Define an application struct to hold the application-wide dependencies for the
// web application. For now we'll only include fields for the two custom loggers, but
// we'll add more to it as the build progresses.
type application struct {
    errorLog *log.Logger
    infoLog  *log.Logger
}

func main() {
    ...
    // Initialize a new instance of our application struct, containing the
    // dependencies.
    app := &application{
        errorLog: errorLog,
        infoLog:  infoLog,
    }

    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    fileServer := http.FileServer(http.Dir("./ui/static/"))
    mux.Handle("/static/", http.StripPrefix("/static", fileServer))

    mux.HandleFunc("/", app.home)
    mux.HandleFunc("/snippet/view", app.snippetView)
    mux.HandleFunc("/snippet/create", app.snippetCreate)
    ...
}
File: cmd/web/handlers.go — methods, not functionsgo
// Change the signature of the home handler so it is defined as a method against
// *application.
func (app *application) home(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    ...
    ts, err := template.ParseFiles(files...)
    if err != nil {
        // Because the home handler function is now a method against application
        // it can access its fields, including the error logger. We'll write the log
        // message to this instead of the standard logger.
        app.errorLog.Print(err.Error())
        http.Error(w, "Internal Server Error", 500)
        return
    }
    ...
}

It looks like ceremony for two loggers — and the book admits as much — but the pattern pays off as the struct grows. To prove it works, the book deliberately breaks the app: rename home.tmpl and request the home page.

Terminalshell
$ mv ui/html/pages/home.tmpl ui/html/pages/home.bak
$ go run ./cmd/web
INFO    2022/01/29 16:12:36 Starting server on :4000
ERROR   2022/01/29 16:12:40 handlers.go:29: open ./ui/html/pages/home.tmpl: no such file or directory

The ERROR prefix and the handlers.go reference prove the logger travelled from main() into the handler as a dependency. (The book leaves the error in place — the next section needs it.)

Additional information. This pattern does not work when handlers live in several packages. The alternative is a config package with an exported Application struct, and handlers as closures: examplePackage.ExampleHandler(app) returns an http.HandlerFunc that closes over the struct.

Live: /break toggles exactly this failure. Switch it on, request /home, and the log shows the ERROR line with the handler’s file and line.

3.4 · Centralized error handling

Error handling now repeats itself in every handler. Three small helpers on the application struct fix that — serverError logs the error plus a stack trace and sends a generic 500, clientError sends any 4xx/5xx with its standard description, and notFound wraps the 404 case.

File: cmd/web/helpers.gogo
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "net/http"
    "runtime/debug"
)

// The serverError helper writes an error message and stack trace to the errorLog,
// then sends a generic 500 Internal Server Error response to the user.
func (app *application) serverError(w http.ResponseWriter, err error) {
    trace := fmt.Sprintf("%s\n%s", err.Error(), debug.Stack())
    app.errorLog.Print(trace)
    http.Error(w, http.StatusText(http.StatusInternalServerError), http.StatusInternalServerError)
}

// The clientError helper sends a specific status code and corresponding description
// to the user. We'll use this later in the book to send responses like 400 "Bad
// Request" when there's a problem with the request that the user sent.
func (app *application) clientError(w http.ResponseWriter, status int) {
    http.Error(w, http.StatusText(status), status)
}

// For consistency, we'll also implement a notFound helper. This is simply a
// convenience wrapper around clientError which sends a 404 Not Found response to
// the user.
func (app *application) notFound(w http.ResponseWriter) {
    app.clientError(w, http.StatusNotFound)
}

debug.Stack() captures the current goroutine’s execution path, which is what makes an error message debuggable; http.StatusText() turns 400 into "Bad Request" for you. The handlers then shrink to calls like app.serverError(w, err), app.notFound(w) and app.clientError(w, http.StatusMethodNotAllowed).

The first attempt has a flaw. The log line now reports helpers.go:13 — the place the message is written — rather than the handler that hit the error:

Terminal — wrong originshell
$ go run ./cmd/web
INFO    2022/01/29 16:22:14 Starting server on :4000
ERROR   2022/01/29 16:22:19 helpers.go:13: open ./ui/html/pages/home.tmpl: no such file or directory
goroutine 6 [running]:
runtime/debug.Stack()
        /usr/local/go/src/runtime/debug/stack.go:24 +0x65
main.(*application).serverError(...)
        /home/alex/Desktop/snippetbox.v2/cmd/web/helpers.go:12 +0x66
main.(*application).home(...)
        /home/alex/Desktop/snippetbox.v2/cmd/web/handlers.go:24 +0x194
...

The fix is Output() with a calldepth of 2, which tells the logger to report the caller one frame further up:

File: cmd/web/helpers.go — correctedgo
func (app *application) serverError(w http.ResponseWriter, err error) {
    trace := fmt.Sprintf("%s\n%s", err.Error(), debug.Stack())
    app.errorLog.Output(2, trace)
    http.Error(w, http.StatusText(http.StatusInternalServerError), http.StatusInternalServerError)
}
Terminal — correct originshell
$ go run ./cmd/web
INFO    2022/01/29 16:24:00 Starting server on :4000
ERROR   2022/01/29 16:24:02 handlers.go:24: open ./ui/html/pages/home.tmpl: no such file or directory

The deliberate error is no longer needed: mv ui/html/pages/home.bak ui/html/pages/home.tmpl.

3.5 · Isolating the application routes

main() is getting crowded. The route declarations move into their own file, as a method on the application struct:

File: cmd/web/routes.gogo
package main

import "net/http"

// The routes() method returns a servemux containing our application routes.
func (app *application) routes() *http.ServeMux {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()

    fileServer := http.FileServer(http.Dir("./ui/static/"))
    mux.Handle("/static/", http.StripPrefix("/static", fileServer))

    mux.HandleFunc("/", app.home)
    mux.HandleFunc("/snippet/view", app.snippetView)
    mux.HandleFunc("/snippet/create", app.snippetCreate)

    return mux
}
File: cmd/web/main.go — the whole function, at lastgo
func main() {
    addr := flag.String("addr", ":4000", "HTTP network address")

    flag.Parse()

    infoLog := log.New(os.Stdout, "INFO\t", log.Ldate|log.Ltime)
    errorLog := log.New(os.Stderr, "ERROR\t", log.Ldate|log.Ltime|log.Lshortfile)

    app := &application{
        errorLog: errorLog,
        infoLog:  infoLog,
    }

    srv := &http.Server{
        Addr:     *addr,
        ErrorLog: errorLog,
        // Call the new app.routes() method to get the servemux containing our routes.
        Handler: app.routes(),
    }

    infoLog.Printf("Starting server on %s", *addr)
    err := srv.ListenAndServe()
    errorLog.Fatal(err)
}

And with that, main() does exactly three things: parse configuration, establish dependencies, run the server. Everything else now has a home.
